newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany vows to hold line on Scientology.
newsitem.headline: Germany vows to hold line on Scientology.

text.p: Germany vowed on Friday it would not change its tough stance towards the Church of Scientology despite U.S. criticism, saying its Nazi past meant it had to be especially vigilant in monitoring totalitarian groups.

Government spokesman Peter Hausmann said the U.S. State Department's annual human rights survey showed there were differences of opinion on how to deal with Scientology, but that Germany was obliged to take a tough line.
Asked if Bonn would change its attitude in the light of the report, Hausmann said: "Experiences with totalitarianism have influenced us and still influence our attitude here."
"These experiences have found their expression in our constitution and from that comes the obligation to be especially vigilant against totalitarian and anti-democratic tendencies."

The U.S. report documented in detail Scientologists' allegations of persecution and discrimination in Germany. A senior State Department official said it represented Washington's "serious concern" over the issue.
The head of the Church of Scientology in Los Angeles hailed the report as "the most decisive condemnation of German human rights terrorism since the end of World War Two".
But Hausmann told reporters Bonn could be proud of its human rights record, which stood up well to international comparison.

"It is the obligation of all public bodies to protect the human dignity of its citizens. That includes their physical and mental safety," Hausmann said. "The German government will continue to do that."
The latest annual survey was the fifth to document Germany's treatment of Scientology, a religious philosophy founded in 1954 by U.S. science fiction writer L. Ron Hubbard.

Germany does not accord Scientology the status of a religion, believing it to be a purely economic organisation which exploits the insecurities of its members to make big profits from expensive self-improvement courses.

The southern state of Bavaria has been at the forefront of the fight against Scientology, excluding companies run by Scientologists from public tenders and asking applicants for public sector jobs whether they belong to the group.
It has also placed Scientology under observation by the state's anti-extremist watchdog.
Germany's stance on Scientologists joins China's suppression of opposition groups, Turkey's treatment of its Kurdish minority and Indonesian clampdowns in East Timor in the U.S. survey.

"I don't understand this at all," said Peter Hintze, general secretary of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats. "The U.S. is applying a level of tolerance which takes no account of possible dangers and you can't deal with psycho-sects like that.
"We must say quite clearly to our American partners that a dressing-down of this sort is not the right thing to do for partners within a common alliance."
Hintze received strong backing from the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who said the German government should protest to Washington about the way it is portrayed in the report.
"Scientology is an organisation which pursues murky aims by applying pressure and sometimes psycho-terror," said Guenter Verheugen, the SPD's deputy leader in parliament.

Bavaria and its neighbouring state of Baden-Wuerttemberg on Friday began a fresh chapter in their battle with Scientology by introducing a parliamentary motion on the subject, which will be discussed over the next few weeks.

The motion in the upper house calls on the government to raise problems with the group at international level and to investigate whether it even deserves the status of an association which it currently enjoys in Germany.
